extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes procedural rules, ceremonial practices, and notable descriptive 'rules' or set-pieces from a chapter of Rabelais' Gargantua and Pantagruel (Queen Whims / Entelechy episodes). Useful for literary analysis or adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queen Whims' method of curing (song/organ)
rubrics_metrics.description: “our queen cures all manner of diseases without so much as touching the sick, but barely with a song, according to the nature of the distemper.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cures are performed by the queen singing while touching an organ (described: "pipes were of cassia fistula in the cod; the top and cornice of guiacum; the bellows of rhubarb; the pedas of turbith, and the clavier or keys of scammony"). Leprous, poisoned, deaf, blind, and dumb patients are brought in and are immediately cured by her song; examples include leprous cured on the spot, poisoned persons recovering use of their legs, and restoration of senses. The queen also uses a nosegay to restore Pantagruel’s senses after the spectacle. Surrounding explanation emphasizes marvel and theatricality (officers such as abstractors, spodizators, etc., assist in the process).

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal dining protocol (praegustators and masticators)
rubrics_metrics.description: “When her praegustators had tasted the meat, her masticators took it and chewed it most nobly; ... they poured it down her throat through a funnel of fine gold, and so on to her craw.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The queen herself chews nothing; designated officers (praegustators taste, masticators chew) prepare the food which is then funneled to the queen. She eats only 'celestial ambrosia' and drinks 'divine nectar'; her household uses elaborate ritual and proxy consumption (the text notes she 'never visited a close-stool but by proxy'). The passage is presented as ceremonial protocol, emphasizing absurd ceremonial specialization and social satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ball/tournament dance rules and choreography
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed staging: thirty-two participants arranged in two bands (sixteen in cloth of gold, sixteen in cloth of silver). Kings and queens are placed on specified squares of a large chequered tapestry (three spans wide squares); musicians (eight per side) play different instruments; dancers perform varied steps and respond to musical notes by taking designated squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific movement rules for the nymphs: they march forward from square to square, never fall back (except the first step may move two squares), and if a nymph reaches the opposite king’s row she is crowned queen of that king and thereafter moves as a queen. The choreography maps musical cues to precise positions and movements (many named steps: bounds, rebounds, jerks, paces, leaps, skips, turns, coupes, hops, leadings, risings, meetings, flights, ambuscadoes, moves, removes). The arrangement and rule set function like a stylized game/tournament—music determines placement and status changes (promotion to queen) based on reaching specified rows.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of revived ancient dances/sports (ceremonial program)
rubrics_metrics.description: “We also perceived how they revived ancient sports, diverting themselves together at-- 1. Cordax. 2. Emmelia. 3. Sicinnia. 4. Jambics. 5. Persica. 6. Phrygia. 7. Thracia. 8. Calabrisme. 9. Molossia. 10. Cernophorum. 11. Monogas. 12. Terminalia. 13. Floralia. 14. Pyrrhice. 15. (Nicatism.) And a thousand other dances.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motteux footnote supplies brief glosses for many items (e.g., Cordax: a sort of country-dance; Emmelia: a still tragic dance; Sicinnia: dancing and singing used at funerals; Floralia: dancing naked at Flora’s holidays; Pyrrhice: the Trojan dance in armour). The list functions as a ceremonial program: naming canonical/archaic dance forms and implying associated atmospheres and ritual meanings. Useful for scholars seeking parody targets or dance/gaming motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrations of pseudo-scientific offices and occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous household officers perform absurd, impossible, or satirical feats: making blackamoors white by rubbing bellies with a pannier, extracting water from pumice by braying it, shearing asses to get long fleece wool, pitching nets to catch the wind, making chalk of cheese, honey of a dog’s t--d, getting farts out of a dead ass and selling them, measuring flea leaps to govern kingdoms, guarding the moon from wolves, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The catalogue of occupations and experiments reads as a litany of satire on pseudo-science, alchemy, and courtly specialization. Some items are presented as cures (e.g., curing pox by touching dentiform vertebrae thrice with a wooden shoe; curing dropsy by striking the belly nine times with a Tenedian hatchet; curing gout by making the patient shut his mouth and open his eyes). The surrounding prose frames these as official offices and profitable trades—useful when analyzing Rabelais’ critique of learned professions, pseudo-experimentation, or ritualized court functions.
